q: Transaction A updates row 1 and has not committed. What can another transaction do with row 1?
options: Read it with a plain SELECT. It cannot update the row until A finishes
Nothing at all, even reading waits
Update it at the same time
Delete it, but not update it
why: A row lock stops other writers of that row. It does not stop readers, and it does not stop writers of other rows.

options: Updates the rows to a new value
Locks the selected rows, so nobody else can change them until you finish
Blocks every plain SELECT on the table
Makes the query faster
why: Use it when you read a row and then decide what to write.

q: Which option makes a query skip rows that another transaction has locked?
options: `NOWAIT`
`lock_timeout`
`SKIP LOCKED`
`FOR SHARE`
why: NOWAIT fails at once. SKIP LOCKED skips locked rows. lock_timeout gives up after a time.

q: Transaction A locks row 1 then row 2. Transaction B locks row 2 then row 1. What happens?
options: Both finish normally
Both wait for ever
Postgres merges the two transactions
A deadlock. Postgres cancels one of them, and your code must retry it
why: A deadlock is a circle of waiting.

q: How do you avoid most deadlocks?
options: Lock rows in one fixed order (for example ORDER BY id) and keep transactions short
Use a bigger connection pool
Run every query twice
Use READ UNCOMMITTED
why: If everyone locks in the same order, nobody can wait in a circle.

q: An `ALTER TABLE` is waiting for a lock. Why can plain reads of that table get stuck behind it?
options: ALTER TABLE rewrites all indexes at once
The waiting ALTER TABLE is in the line, and new readers queue behind it
Reads are always blocked by DDL
Postgres closes all connections
why: Run migrations with a short lock_timeout, so a waiting ALTER gives up instead of blocking the site.
